t: Maximum Sum Score of Array — Prefix and Suffix Sums in One Pass
o: For each index $i$ we compare two quantities: the sum of the first $i+1$ elements and the sum of the last $n-i$ elements, and we want the largest value of max(front, back) over all indices. In Example 1 ([4,3,-2,5]) the total is 10, so index 0 scores max(4, 10) = 10 and index 3 also scores max(10, 5) = 10; the answer is 10. In Example 2 ([-3,-5]) every candidate is negative, and the best is -3 at index 0. With $n$ up to $10^5$, recomputing both sums from scratch for every index ($O(n^2)$) is too slow in the worst case, which hints at precomputing prefix/suffix sums. Note values can be negative, so the answer may be negative and sums can reach plus or minus $10^{10}$, requiring a 64-bit accumulator.
k: The suffix sum ending consideration at index $i$ equals the total sum minus the prefix sum of the first $i$ elements, so no separate suffix array is needed.
Because elements can be negative, initialize the answer to negative infinity rather than 0, and use 64-bit integers since totals reach $10^{10}$.
A single running prefix variable turns this into one clean pass over the array.

a.i: Directly follow the definition: for each index, loop twice to add up the front part and the back part, then take their max. This is the most literal translation of the problem statement and needs no extra insight, but each of the $n$ indices costs $O(n)$ summation work.
s: For each index i from 0 to n-1, compute front = nums[0..i] and back = nums[i..n-1].
Update best with max(best, front, back).
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n indices we rescan up to 2n elements.
a.sp: O(1) — only scalar accumulators are used.

a.n: Approach 2: One-Pass Prefix/Suffix via Total Sum
a.i: Compute the total once. While sweeping left to right keep a running prefix that after adding nums[i] equals the front sum at index i; the corresponding back sum is total - prefix + nums[i]. Taking the max of both candidates at every index gives the answer in a single pass with constant extra space — strictly better than maintaining two arrays.
s: For each element x: prefix += x; candidate back = total - prefix + x.
Answer = max(answer, prefix, total - prefix + x).
a.t: O(n) — one pass to compute the total plus one pass over the array.
a.sp: O(1) — just the running prefix and the total.

w: In an interview, state the brute force first, then derive the O(n) version by noticing back(i) = total - front(i) + nums[i]. Pitfalls: initializing the answer to 0 fails on all-negative arrays like [-3,-5], and 32-bit sums overflow for n = 10^5 elements of magnitude 10^5 (use long/long long). At the last index front = total, and at index 0 back = total, so the full-array sum is always a candidate. A likely follow-up is returning the index achieving the maximum score instead of the score itself.
